segments.text: Hi everyone, thanks for coming, I know this is the slot right after lunch so I will try to keep you awake.
My name is Priya and I run a very small Kubernetes cluster in a closet at our office.
It is four machines running k3s, and today I want to tell you what happened the night one of them died.
So first, a little background on why we run k3s at all instead of a managed service.
We are a team of six, our budget is small, and we wanted to learn how the pieces fit together.
k3s gave us a single binary, a sane default storage class, and Traefik out of the box.
For about a year it just worked, and honestly we stopped paying much attention to it.
Then one Tuesday night the power supply in node three gave up with a very sad little click.
The first thing we noticed was not an alert, it was a customer saying the site felt slow.
That is lesson number one, and I will come back to it: we had no alert for a missing node.
Kubernetes did notice, of course, but it noticed on its own schedule, not ours.
By default a node is marked not ready after about forty seconds without a heartbeat.
Then the pods on that node wait roughly five more minutes before they get evicted.
So for five minutes, a third of our app replicas were sitting on a machine that no longer existed.
The service still sent traffic to them until the endpoints were updated, which is why things felt slow.
Lesson number two is that readiness probes are doing more work than you think.
Our app replicas came back on other nodes fairly quickly once eviction kicked in.
The database was a different story, and this is where most of my gray hair comes from.
We ran Postgres as a StatefulSet with a local path volume, which means the data lives on one disk.
When that disk is inside a dead machine, the pod cannot just move somewhere else.
Kubernetes was very polite about it and simply refused to schedule the pod anywhere.
So we had a database that was technically configured, and practically gone.
Luckily we had nightly backups to object storage, and we had actually tested restoring them once.
I cannot stress that enough, a backup you have never restored is just a hopeful file.
We restored to a new volume on node one and lost about nine hours of writes.
Nine hours sounds bad, and it was, but for our app it meant some draft notes and a few comments.
Afterwards we sat down and wrote down what we would change, and I want to walk through that list.
First, we spread the app replicas across machines with topology spread constraints.
Before, the scheduler had happily put two of our three replicas on the same node.
Second, we added a pod disruption budget so a drain never takes every replica at once.
Third, we added an alert on node not ready that pages someone after two minutes.
Fourth, and this is the big one, we moved backups from nightly to every fifteen minutes.
We looked at running replicated storage like Longhorn, and maybe we will get there.
But for a cluster this size, more storage software was more things to break at two in the morning.
Write ahead log shipping every fifteen minutes gave us most of the benefit for very little effort.
We also practice now, which sounds silly, but we literally unplug a machine once a month.
The first time we did it on purpose, it took us forty minutes to recover the database.
The last time it took six, because we had a written runbook and we had done it before.
I want to show you that runbook quickly, it is only one page and it fits on the screen.
Step one, confirm the node is really gone and not just a network blip.
Step two, cordon it so nothing new lands there when it comes back confused.
Step three, restore the latest base backup and replay the logs onto a fresh volume.
Step four, point the StatefulSet at the new volume and watch the app reconnect.
That is all of it, and the whole point is that a tired person at night can follow it.
The other thing I want to say is that small clusters are not toys.
They fail in exactly the same ways as big ones, you just have less room to hide.
So, to sum up: alert on nodes, spread your replicas, back up often, and practice the restore.
That is my talk, thank you so much, and I think we have a few minutes for questions.
Okay, I see a hand in the front, go ahead.
Um, so what actually happens to the traffic when a node dies, like during those first few minutes?
So the question is what happens to traffic in the first few minutes after a node dies.
The short answer is that some requests still go to the dead pods until Kubernetes takes them out of the endpoints.
Readiness probes help a lot there, and so does having replicas on other machines so the healthy ones keep serving.
Great, next question, over there by the door.
Did you ever think about just paying for a managed database instead of running Postgres yourselves?
Yeah, we did, and honestly for most teams I would say just pay for it.
For us it was about learning and about cost, our whole cluster costs less than one managed database instance.
Hi, how long did it take you to write the runbook, and who keeps it up to date?
The first version took an afternoon, and whoever runs the monthly unplug drill fixes anything that was wrong.
So, yeah, the drill is what keeps it honest, a runbook nobody runs goes stale really fast.
One more maybe, in the back.
Why not run three Postgres replicas with something like an operator, so a node failure is automatic?
So the question is why not use a Postgres operator with replicas, and that is a fair question.
We tried one and it worked, but we did not understand it well enough to fix it when it broke, so we chose boring.
Alright, I think that is time, thanks again everyone.

speaker: Priya Natarajan
title: Surviving a node failure on a small k3s cluster (sample)
